column1: Create a view with {{c1::CREATE VIEW}} Sales.ActiveCustomers AS SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName FROM Sales.Customers WHERE IsActive = 1;
column2:
An ordinary view defines a query rather than storing a separate result set.
Review source

column1: Define a view's query with CREATE VIEW Sales.CustomerNames {{c1::AS}} SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName FROM Sales.Customers;
column2:
The SELECT statement determines the view's rows and columns.
Review source

column1: A view can hide a reusable {{c1::JOIN}} between customer and order tables behind one queryable object.
column2:
Callers do not need to repeat the join in every application query.
Review source

column1: A view can calculate an order category with {{c1::CASE}} WHEN TotalAmount < 100 THEN 'Small' ELSE 'Other' END AS OrderSize.
column2:
This keeps the categorization expression in the view definition.
Review source

column1: A calculated expression exposed by a view needs a {{c1::column name}}, supplied by an alias or the view's column list.
column2:
For example, END AS OrderSize names a CASE expression's result.
Review source

column1: For an updatable filtered view, place {{c1::WITH CHECK OPTION}} after the SELECT query to enforce visibility after INSERT or UPDATE.
column2:
Example: CREATE VIEW Sales.HighValueOrders AS SELECT OrderID, TotalAmount FROM Sales.Orders WHERE TotalAmount > 1000 WITH CHECK OPTION;
Review source

column1: An otherwise valid INSERT of TotalAmount = 500 through a view filtered by TotalAmount > 1000 WITH CHECK OPTION is {{c1::rejected}}.
column2:
The inserted row would not be visible through the view.
Review source

column1: WITH CHECK OPTION checks changes made {{c1::through the view}}, not changes made directly to its base tables.
column2:
The option is not a table-wide integrity constraint.
Review source

column1: To use a view as a restricted data interface, grant access to it while restricting direct access to {{c1::its base tables}}.
column2:
Other permissions can provide an access path that bypasses the view.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, the first index that materializes a view must be a {{c1::unique clustered index}}.
column2:
The view must also use WITH SCHEMABINDING and satisfy the other indexed-view requirements.
Review source

column1: Indexed views can increase base-table write costs because SQL Server must also {{c1::maintain the views' stored results}}.
column2:
Evaluate this maintenance cost rather than assuming materialization improves every workload.
Review source

column1: To guarantee sorted results when querying a SQL Server view, put ORDER BY in {{c1::the outer SELECT query}}.
column2:
Ordering inside a view, where allowed for TOP or OFFSET, does not guarantee the caller's result order.
Review source
